name: Jute mallow
summary: How Filipino growers, Ilocanos above all, usually raise saluyot from seed scattered at the start of the rains and pick the young tops again and again for weeks. For backyard and small market growers who want the usual way and simple steps for more tender leaves.
season: Saluyot loves warm, humid weather and is usually sown when the rains come, around May to June, often near rivers and creeks. With water it can be grown in other months. Cold spells and long droughts stunt or kill it. The biggest growing areas are in Ilocos and Western Visayas.
material: Seed, from a plant left to ripen its pods. The seed is tiny and has a hard coat, so many growers pour hot water over it briefly, then cool it, before sowing so it sprouts evenly. There is a purplish type (pula) and a light green type (puti). The green one is preferred by many city buyers.
spacing: Seed is scattered thinly or drilled in shallow rows, and crowded seedlings are thinned by hand so each plant has room to branch. Many backyard plots also come up on their own from seed dropped by last year's plants.
water: Rainfed in the wet season. Watered every day or two in dry spells. Saluyot takes heat but not long droughts, and it grows best on moist ground near water.
fertilizer: Mostly compost or rotted manure in the soil, with manure tea or a little urea after the picking rounds to keep new tops coming.
care: Thinning, a weeding or two while the plants are small, steady moisture, and frequent picking of the tops, which keeps the plants bushy and tender. Some plants are left to flower and pod for next season's seed.
harvest: The first tops are picked about five to six weeks after sowing, then every week or two for as long as the plants stay leafy. Growers pick in the cool hours, tie the tops in bundles and keep them shaded and moist.

ways.label: Seed scattered on the plot (sabog tanim)

steps.title: Loosen the soil and add manure
steps.how: Dig or plow the plot and mix in compost or rotted manure. Loam or silty loam near water is best, but saluyot grows in most soils.

steps.title: Treat the seed
steps.how: Put the seed in a cloth, dip it briefly in hot water, then in cool water, and let it dry a little so it is easy to scatter.
steps.tip: Mix the tiny seed with fine sand so it spreads thinly.

steps.title: Scatter or drill the seed
steps.how: Scatter the seed thinly over the plot or drop it in shallow rows, rake lightly and water, or sow right after a good rain.

steps.title: Keep the plot moist
steps.how: Water every day or two until the seedlings are up and growing well. Do not let the young plants dry out.

steps.title: Thin and weed
steps.how: Pull out crowded seedlings, which can be cooked, and the weeds, so the rest have room to branch.

steps.title: Check the leaves
steps.how: Look for leaf eating caterpillars, beetles and mites under the leaves and pick off badly damaged shoots.

steps.title: Pick the young tops
steps.how: When the plants are knee high, about five to six weeks after sowing, pinch or cut the tender tops and young leaves. This makes the plant branch out.

steps.title: Feed and keep picking
steps.how: After each picking, side dress with compost, manure tea or a little urea, water, and come back for the new tops every week or two.

steps.title: Bundle and keep cool
steps.how: Tie the tops in bundles and keep them shaded and sprinkled with water, because the leaves wilt fast.

mistakes: Sowing the hard seed untreated, so it comes up thin and uneven.
Sowing too thick and never thinning, so the plants grow tall and spindly with few tops.
Letting the plants dry out, which makes them flower early and the leaves tough.
Letting the plants run tall without picking, so leaves get fewer and harder.
Picking in the noon heat and leaving the bundles in the sun.
better: Use seed from your best, leafiest plants or a good variety, and treat it before sowing.
Add compost and a balanced fertilizer by soil test instead of urea alone.
Sow in steps every few weeks so there are tops to sell all season.
Keep moisture steady with mulch and water in dry spells.
Pick tops on a regular schedule and keep the bundles cool to market.

watering.traditional: Saluyot is mostly a rain crop, sown when the rains come around May to June, often on moist ground near rivers and creeks. In dry spells growers water every day or two by can or hose, and with water it grows well even in the summer months.
watering.method: Mostly rain. Watering cans and hoses on small plots, furrows on bigger ones. Water in the morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Sow when the rains come, around May to June, on loam or silty ground near a river or creek that stays moist. Thin the stand so the plants do not compete for water, and mulch with straw or cut grass if the rains break.
watering.dryseason: In the summer months saluyot grows well only when watered every day or two. Water when the leaves droop by mid morning or the top soil is dry.
watering.wet: Saluyot likes wet weather but not standing water. Sow on ground that drains and open small canals in low spots so the young plants do not rot.

schedule.often: Sow right after a good rain or water the plot after sowing, then every day or two until the seedlings are up
schedule.amount: A gentle watering that keeps the top soil damp without washing the seed
schedule.why: The small seed sits near the surface and dies if the top soil dries.

schedule.often: Water every day or two in dry spells. Water before thinning so the extra plants pull out easily
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the soil moist to the roots
schedule.why: Young saluyot stunts or dies if it dries out.

schedule.often: Keep the soil moist, every day or two in dry weather
schedule.why: Steady moisture gives tender, leafy tops.

schedule.often: Water after each picking and feeding, and every day or two in dry spells
schedule.why: The plants branch and give new tops only with water and feeding. Long droughts make them flower and turn woody.

critical: Sowing to the young plants: the plot must not dry out.
Long dry spells at any stage, which stunt or kill saluyot.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and yellow, the plants stay short and flower early, and the tops turn tough.
signs.wet: Seedlings rot at the base in waterlogged spots and the lower leaves yellow.

better: Water and feed right after each picking so the plants branch and give more tops.
Mulch the plot to hold moisture through dry spells.
